target_customer: Homeowners and developers buying prefabricated 3D printed accessory dwelling units and homes, mainly in California
problem: Construction is slow, labor intensive and wasteful; the company printed wall and building panels with robots in a factory and assembled homes from them.
business_model: Sells prefab homes and panel kits built in its own factory

founders.name: Slava Solonitsyn
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him under former founders; the company says it was founded by physicists and robotics engineers.

founders.name: Dmitry Starodubtsev
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him under former founders.

founders.name: Alexey Dubov
founders.background_notes: Named as co-founder and COO in the TechCrunch article of 2021-02-09; not on the YC page.

exit.reason: Restructured and put up for sale through Rock Creek Advisors in January 2025; no stated financial reason

competitors.name: Apis Cor
competitors.what: Mobile on-site 3D printer that printed a 38 square meter house in Stupino, Russia
competitors.traction_then: One demonstration house reported at about 10,134 USD cost

technical_complexity.rationale: It needed a new UV curing composite material, robotic printing and factory automation, plus building code approval, which is hardware and materials research for a small team.

defensibility.rationale: The company cites its own composite material and building certifications (California factory built housing, UL 3401), but a factory with high fixed costs and no stated patents in opened sources limits the moat.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Rivals built on site rather than copying the factory model; the company itself ran out of runway by 2025 and was put up for sale.

market_need_then: California faced a housing shortage and accessory dwelling unit rules were loosening; the sources cited describe the aim of faster cheaper homes, but no demand figures from 2018 were found.

branding.domain_note: Uses mightybuildings.com; no purchase history found.

identity.logo: Wordmark with an MB mark per trademark filings
identity.visual_style: Design press describes sleek modern prefab homes
identity.voice_and_tone: Mission led, focused on sustainability and the housing crisis

branding.brand_signature: 3D printed homes made of Light Stone Material
branding.community_and_virality: Covered by design and tech press (Dwell, TechCrunch, Design Milk); no fan community found.

brand_strength.rationale: Repeated coverage in design and tech outlets and a YC top company listing made it recognizable in the 3D printed housing niche, but no evidence the brand drove sales.

outcome_analysis: Mighty Buildings raised about 150 million dollars from 2018 to 2023 for a capital heavy factory model that printed homes from a custom composite. After a 52 million dollar round in September 2023 it restructured and in January 2025 announced it was for sale, citing a wider contraction in additive construction. The company gave no explicit financial reason, so the failure factors are inferences from the sale, the sector downturn that the article cites and the high cost of the model.
notes: Company site returned HTTP 503. Exit type is unknown, not shutdown: the company was for sale in 2025 and one listing says Mighty Buildings is now a brand of LUMUS (single source, unverified); YC marks it inactive. The 2018 seed ($10M) rests on SeedTable alone and the 2019 Series A (~$26M) on aggregators (StartupIntros, ZoomInfo) alone. Round sizes sum to about 150M, matching the 150M total TechCrunch cited in 2023, and 100M total stated in July 2021 is consistent. The 2021-07 and 2023-09 rounds have stage labels that conflict across databases (Series B or C), so stage is other. Another listing names Sam Ruben as a fourth co-founder (single search snippet, not used). Education and prior employers not found in opened sources. ICON (a $35M Series A in Aug 2020) emerged later and is not listed as a competitor.
